extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, creative_writing students, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing narrative method (scenic vs pictorial), preparing and executing climaxes, and managing point of view in novels so that character motivation and dramatic effect are convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax should be free to do what it must
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax's task is only to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; it should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare earlier stages so the climax need only supply the necessary movement that declares and fulfils the book's intention. Avoid loading the climax with tasks or explanatory material that could be dealt with beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax as pictorial impression requiring time
rubrics_metrics.description: Some climaxes are not single dramatic incidents but pictorial impressions of change and decay that need time and gradual development (example: Eugenie Grandet's slow chill of hope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the climax is an impression rather than a single stroke, lead into it gradually and provide ample time and buildup so a brief summary at the moment of climax suffices. Don't force sudden revelations where slow accumulation is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the climax from deliberate expatiation (economy of preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax should be saved from the burden of deliberate expatiation; the art of preparation is no art if it betrays itself at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold back effects until the right page; create and reserve an effect so that when used later it appears inevitable and unforced. If preparation calls attention to itself, it spoils the pleasure and weakens the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amass reserve of effect in opening picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the opening descriptive picture to gather the reserve of effect needed later (Balzac's method: build a richly created world which can be gradually denuded and destroyed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a detailed, stable world (household, possessions, status) early so later loss and repetition of setbacks renew and increase dramatic force. A richly rendered beginning provides material whose deterioration intensifies the story's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained repetition for fixed-idea stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is the growth of a fixed idea (a single, recurring effect), the book must remain on that straight, sustained movement reiterating one effect with growing intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting development via varied incidents; instead heighten the same suspense and shock repeatedly at increasing pitch to dramatize progressive ruin or obsession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject: 'The subject dictates the method.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose scenic (immediate action) or pictorial/retrospective (generalized description) method according to what the subject demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply a favorite method regardless of subject. If the theme is best served by scene-after-scene drama, use a scenic plan; if it needs a broad pictorial impression and reserve-of-effect, use descriptive/retrospective handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a story's turning-point is the start, condense and concentrate presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the turning-point that begins the action requires full knowledge of the character's life, the opening must be tightly packed and concentrated to render 'all that is to be expressed at once.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely scenic exposition that plunges into a crisis before the character's life and motives are clearly conveyed. Use condensed, pictorial preparation (Balzac-like) when the story starts on a critical height of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting at a crisis without adequate internal preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a story on the protagonist's crisis (as Tolstoy does with Anna) risks making the action seem arbitrary if the reader has not been given enough of the character's life and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the reader can gauge the force of a protagonist's action by providing sufficient background or concentrated portrayal of the life and circumstances that produced it; otherwise the crisis lacks fateful importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use point of view to dramatize and to locate authorial authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of fiction is governed by point of view; bringing a narrator into the story (a spokesman) dramatizes the author and reduces arbitrary assertion by making responsibility visible and measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider dramatizing the narrator (or shifting to a spokesman) so statements are anchored in a recognizable voice within the scene. Doing so can make assertions feel self-contained and less externally imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: For exploration of a consciousness, show the mind at work (present enactment over retrospective report)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story's subject is the narrator or a character's own consciousness, an after-the-fact account in the character's words is inferior to presenting the mind in action while agitation is occurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer techniques that let the reader witness thought and feeling as they are formed (objective enactment, interior scenes) rather than relying solely on retrospective narration that reports how the mind was affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress toward dramatization: move from author-report to direct enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer can progress from telling as an external narrator, to placing a spokesman in the story, to finally letting the reader witness the action directly as it passes, avoiding explanation and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shifts of point of view to increase immediacy when the subject demands. Stop expounding and instead let scenes enact the story; place the reader at the angle of vision of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: For purely dramatic subjects, keep strictly scenic form
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely dramatic subject tells itself in strict tightness: one occasion or episode follows another with no interruption for reflective summary or generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overarching generalizations or retrospective reflections that interrupt the scenic flow. Let the scene proceed; the play ceases between scenes and reopens at the next occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brief vivid scenes to create and enrich character (Tolstoy's half-page scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, vividly rendered scenes (a child's action, an incidental domestic detail) can become poetic events that enrich character and are not mere diversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ compact, evocative episodes to add tone and reality to characters; these enrich the reader's impression and can propel the story by augmenting the lives of the figures being watched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when varying method within a crowded structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may vary method (entering consciousness, scenic immediacy, descriptive retrospection) within a book, but inconsistencies of method must be dominated by a clear overall plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use mixed methods, ensure the main structural lines are simple enough to absorb methodical liberties without creating confusion or weakening the intended effect.
